SkillSpec: Consensus-Gated Agent Skill
Evolution via Representation Specialization

Huancheng Chen   Xiaodi Sun   Zhaoqiong Huang   Shenyang Huang   Shreya Singhal   Jingwen Lu

Microsoft AI

Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use natural-language skills to retain and reuse task knowledge without updating model weights. A skill is a textual procedural memory that encodes reusable steps, task rules, tool-use guidance, answer formats, and error-recovery strategies while remaining easy to inspect and revise. However, a fixed skill cannot anticipate every task-specific failure: execution trajectories may reveal missing procedures, conflicting guidance, or underspecified constraints. Recent methods therefore treat prompts and skills as optimizable state [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], replacing one-shot construction with iterative revision informed by execution feedback.

SkillOpt [6] takes an important step toward controlled skill evolution through bounded, validation-gated edits to a trainable skill document. Nevertheless, aggregate validation scores can obscure an edit’s behavioral effects: improvements on some examples may conceal regressions on others, and apparent gains may not persist across repeated evaluations. Existing optimizers also preserve a single-document representation, changing only its wording while leaving the organization of knowledge fixed. Flat representations can obscure procedural dependencies in sequential tasks, whereas unnecessary structure can introduce spurious dependencies and irrelevant context. Our key observation is that deciding what knowledge to retain and how to organize it are distinct optimization problems. The former requires reliable evidence that an edit improves behavior, whereas the latter requires evidence about procedural dependencies and interference. Addressing both in a single rewriting loop makes it difficult to attribute gains or choose an appropriate representation.

We introduce SkillSpec, a two-phase framework that separates reliable content evolution from representation specialization. In the first phase, SkillSpec generates candidate skills under four complementary editing intents: repair, preserve, simplify, and rewrite. It compares each candidate with the current skill on the same validation instances. The consensus gate accepts an update only when it improves performance overall with non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation, while retaining evidence from rejected candidates to inform representation specialization. Building on the validated skill and the trajectory of candidate evaluations, the second phase estimates process and redundancy sensitivity, then uses these signals to select a flat, graph, or hybrid representation. Phase II preserves the validated backbone as an immutable source and specializes a derived artifact, allowing both its guidance and organization to evolve within the selected representation.

We evaluate SkillSpec on six benchmarks, SearchQA [7], DocVQA [8], LiveMath [9], ALFWorld [10], SpreadsheetBench [11], and OfficeQA [12], using three frontier language models. Across the six benchmarks, SkillSpec improves average success rate over the no-skill baseline by up to 24.59%. Compared with SkillOpt [6], SkillSpec yields gains of 11.63%, 5.92%, and 3.12% for GPT–4.1, GPT–5.4 Nano, and GPT–5.4, respectively, averaging 6.89% across the three models. These results show the largest gain on GPT–4.1, suggesting that explicit skill evolution and reorganization can remain valuable even when the underlying model is less capable. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce consensus-gated skill evolution, which combines multi-intent candidate generation with paired validation to accept reliable content updates, reject edits that fail the aggregate gain thresholds, and retain evidence from rejected candidates to inform representation specialization.

  • •

    We introduce trajectory-guided specialization, which uses Phase I evidence to select and optimize a flat, graph, or hybrid representation while preserving the validated backbone as an immutable source.

  • •

    We evaluate SkillSpec across six benchmarks and three frontier language models, outperforming SkillOpt [6] by 6.89% on average across the three models.

Related Work

Prompt optimization.

A growing line of work treats natural-language prompts as optimizable artifacts rather than static instructions. Search-based methods use task-level scores to optimize candidate instructions [1, 2], while DSPy compiles prompts and demonstrations for compound LM programs [3]. TextGrad [4] propagates natural-language feedback through a compound system, and GEPA [5] uses reflective trajectory feedback while retaining Pareto-efficient candidates over validation instances. These methods establish execution feedback as a practical optimization signal, but operate on prompts or LM programs rather than persistent agent skills.

Skill evolution.

SkillOpt [6] extends iterative optimization from prompts to persistent skills, using execution trajectories to propose bounded revisions and held-out evaluations to select updates. SkillOpt-Lite [13] replaces tree-based candidate merging with direct revision of file-based trajectories while retaining an independent validation gate. Subsequent methods prioritize candidates with greater refinement potential [14], stabilize update directions and adapt edit budgets [15], or train skill editors directly from execution feedback [16, 17, 18]. Other work repairs weak initial skills [19] or supports long-horizon repository curation [20]. Methods in this line improve how skill content is generated, selected, and maintained within a predefined artifact schema. SkillSpec builds on feedback-driven skill evolution with multi-intent candidates and paired, repeated validation, then reuses outcomes from accepted and rejected candidates to inform representation selection.

Skill representation.

Prior work structures skills at different granularities. Skill-Pro [21] represents an executable skill through initiation, execution, and termination conditions. SkillX [22] builds a multi-level skill hierarchy and iteratively refines its knowledge base, while HyperSkill [23] organizes subtasks and reusable skills in an evolving hypergraph for retrieval and maintenance. Graph-of-Skills [24] instead constructs inter-skill dependency graphs for inference-time structural retrieval, and AIP [25] compiles prose skills into schema-validated execution graphs. Most closely, AutoRefine [26] selects among rules, skills, and bounded subagents by compiling trajectory-derived interventions according to runtime ownership. Unlike methods that adopt a predefined structure or select among artifact types, SkillSpec uses outcome telemetry from accepted and rejected Phase I candidates to select a flat, graph, or hybrid representation for a validated skill before specialization.

SkillSpec: A Two-Phase Framework for Skill Evolution

SkillSpec optimizes an external skill artifact 𝒜\mathcal{A} for a fixed policy model πθ\pi_{\theta} without updating the model parameters θ\theta. For an instance xx, executing πθ\pi_{\theta} conditioned on 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces a trajectory τx​(𝒜)\tau_{x}(\mathcal{A}) and evaluator score s⁡(πθ,x,𝒜)s(\pi_{\theta},x,\mathcal{A}). Training trajectories provide evidence for candidate revisions, while held-out validation outcomes determine which revisions are retained, with the goal of improving performance on unseen test instances.

Given an initial textual artifact Φ0\Phi_{0}, SkillSpec decomposes artifact optimization into content evolution and representation specialization. Phase I uses training and validation evidence to produce a validated textual backbone Φ⋆\Phi^{\star} and an optimization trajectory ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}} containing candidate artifacts, execution evidence, paired gains, and validation decisions. Phase II estimates structural sensitivity from ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}} and selects a representation r⋆∈{​f​l​a​t,​g​r​a​p​h,​h​y​b​r​i​d}r^{\star}\in\{\emph{flat},\emph{graph},\emph{hybrid}\}. It then initializes a representation-specific artifact from Φ⋆\Phi^{\star} and specializes it to obtain 𝒜⋆\mathcal{A}^{\star}. Figure 1 illustrates the two-phase workflow and the artifacts passed from Phase I to Phase II.

Phase I: Consensus-Gated Skill Evolution

Phase I evolves Φ0\Phi_{0} over TT optimization rounds. At each round, the policy model executes the current skill on a training batch. Successful and failed trajectories then guide candidate generation under complementary editing intents. Candidates are screened against the current skill using task-level paired gains, and only updates confirmed across multiple executions are committed. The final skill is returned as the validated backbone Φ⋆\Phi^{\star}.

Collecting execution evidence.

At round tt, the fixed policy model uses the current skill Φt\Phi_{t} to solve a sampled training batch ℬt⊂𝒟tr\mathcal{B}_{t}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Phase I partitions the resulting trajectories into successful and failed executions according to their evaluator outcomes. These trajectories and the associated evaluator feedback form the execution evidence ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} used to propose candidate updates.

Multi-intent candidate generation.

Given ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}, the skill optimizer constructs candidate skills under the intent set 𝒰={​r​e​p​a​i​r,​p​r​e​s​e​r​v​e,​s​i​m​p​l​i​f​y,​r​e​w​r​i​t​e}\mathcal{U}=\{\emph{repair},\emph{preserve},\emph{simplify},\emph{rewrite}\}. Repair adds corrective guidance for recurring failures; preserve retains guidance supported by successful trajectories; simplify removes redundant or conflicting guidance; and rewrite restructures the skill when local edits are insufficient. Each intent yields a complete skill candidate rather than an isolated edit. Compatible changes from different intents can also be combined into an additional candidate. The resulting candidate pool is 𝒮t={ϕ~t,j}j\mathcal{S}_{t}=\{\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j}\}_{j}, where jj indexes the candidates generated at round tt. Keeping these candidates distinct allows Phase I to evaluate each update strategy independently rather than fold all proposed changes into a single rewrite.

Screening with paired outcomes.

Each candidate ϕ~t,j∈𝒮t\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j}\in\mathcal{S}_{t} and the current skill Φt\Phi_{t} are evaluated on the same validation instances. Their evaluator scores are compared for each xi∈𝒟valx_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}, yielding the paired counts

nt,j+\displaystyle n^{+}_{t,j} =∑xi∈𝒟val[s(πθ,xi,ϕ~t,j)>s(πθ,xi,Φt)],\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[s(\pi_{\theta},x_{i},\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j})>s(\pi_{\theta},x_{i},\Phi_{t})\right], (1)
nt,j−\displaystyle n^{-}_{t,j} =∑xi∈𝒟val[s(πθ,xi,ϕ~t,j)<s(πθ,xi,Φt)].\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[s(\pi_{\theta},x_{i},\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j})<s(\pi_{\theta},x_{i},\Phi_{t})\right].

Here, nt,j+n^{+}_{t,j} and nt,j−n^{-}_{t,j} count task-level improvements and regressions, respectively; ties contribute to neither count. Their difference gt,j=nt,j+−nt,j−g_{t,j}=n^{+}_{t,j}-n^{-}_{t,j} is the net paired gain. This comparison reveals regressions that gains on other tasks could mask in an aggregate score. Phase I ranks candidates in descending order of gt,jg_{t,j}, resolves equal gains deterministically, and sends the highest-ranked NfN_{f} candidates to the confirmation stage.

Confirming and committing an update.

For each finalist ϕ~t,j\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j}, let gt,j(k)g_{t,j}^{(k)} denote its paired gain in evaluation k∈{0,…,K}k\in\{0,\ldots,K\} on the complete 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}. We set gt,j(0)=gt,jg_{t,j}^{(0)}=g_{t,j} to reuse the screening result, while k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K index additional confirmation executions. Let GpoolG_{\mathrm{pool}} denote the required pooled gain and GminG_{\min} the minimum gain permitted in any single execution. Candidate ϕ~t,j\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j} is confirmed only if

∑k=0Kgt,j(k)≥Gpoolandmin0≤k≤K⁡gt,j(k)≥Gmin.\sum_{k=0}^{K}g_{t,j}^{(k)}\geq G_{\mathrm{pool}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\min_{0\leq k\leq K}g_{t,j}^{(k)}\geq G_{\min}. (2)

The pooled-gain condition requires sufficient overall improvement, while the minimum-gain condition ensures that every execution meets GminG_{\min}. With Gmin=0G_{\min}=0, this requires non-negative aggregate paired gain in each execution; individual validation instances may still regress. If multiple candidates satisfy both conditions, Phase I selects the candidate with the largest pooled gain, resolves ties deterministically, and denotes it by ϕ~t⋆\widetilde{\phi}_{t}^{\star}. The update is then applied atomically:

Φt+1={ϕ~t⋆,if ​ϕ~t⋆​ passes (2),Φt,otherwise.\Phi_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\phi}_{t}^{\star},&\text{if }\widetilde{\phi}_{t}^{\star}\text{ passes \eqref{eq:a21-gate}},\\ \Phi_{t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3)

Let Ωt\Omega_{t} denote the optimizer state used for candidate generation at round tt. When a candidate is committed, Phase I atomically updates both the skill and this state; otherwise, it retains (Φt,Ωt)(\Phi_{t},\Omega_{t}). After each round, it appends the candidate artifacts, execution evidence, paired gains, and validation decisions to the optimization trajectory. After TT rounds, Phase I returns the validated backbone Φ⋆\Phi^{\star} and complete trajectory ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}}. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full update loop.

Phase II: Telemetry-Guided Structural Specialization

Phase II takes the validated backbone Φ⋆\Phi^{\star} and trajectory ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}} from Phase I. Using ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}}, it estimates structural sensitivity, selects a representation, and specializes a derived artifact initialized from Φ⋆\Phi^{\star} while keeping the Phase I outputs unchanged.

Estimating structural sensitivity from telemetry.

Let ℐI\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}} index the candidates in ΓI\Gamma_{\mathrm{I}} that differ from their round incumbent, pass patch validation, and have a recorded screening gain. We refer to these candidates as eligible and let ν=|ℐI|\nu=|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}|. Phase II summarizes their structural sensitivity as

𝒯=(ψ,ρ),\mathcal{T}=(\psi,\rho), (4)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a trajectory-derived structural profile used to specialize the validated backbone, ψ\psi is process sensitivity, and ρ\rho is redundancy sensitivity.

Tasks differ in how their skill guidance should be organized. For example, SearchQA [7] relies on independently retrievable evidence-selection and answer-extraction guidance, whereas LiveMath [9] benefits from an ordered procedure for formalizing and comparing theorem-style claims. A fixed representation may therefore fail to capture necessary dependencies or impose structure on otherwise independent guidance. SkillSpec captures this trade-off with two signals: process sensitivity measures dependence on ordered steps, while redundancy sensitivity measures vulnerability to duplicated, conflicting, or excessive guidance. Together, these signals guide the choice among flat, graph, and hybrid representations.

Process and redundancy sensitivity estimation.

Each candidate ϕ~t,j\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j}, (t,j)∈ℐI(t,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}, contributes one training tuple (gt,j,pt,j,rt,j,ct,j)(g_{t,j},p_{t,j},r_{t,j},c_{t,j}). The label gt,jg_{t,j} is its screening gain. The process score pt,jp_{t,j} measures whether the revision adds an ordered procedure whose later steps depend on earlier results; the interference score rt,jr_{t,j} measures duplicated, conflicting, irrelevant, or excessively verbose guidance. Both use a four-level rubric: 0 (absent), 1 (weak or local), 2 (clear), and 3 (dominant). The normalized edit size is

ct,j=Dline​(Φt,ϕ~t,j)/max⁡{L⁡(Φt),L⁡(ϕ~t,j)},c_{t,j}=D_{\mathrm{line}}(\Phi_{t},\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j})\,/\,\max\{L(\Phi_{t}),L(\widetilde{\phi}_{t,j})\}, (5)

where DlineD_{\mathrm{line}} counts inserted, deleted, or replaced lines and L⁡(⋅)L(\cdot) denotes the number of lines.

For each benchmark, ridge regression fits a sensitivity function ff to these tuples. Let ft,j​(p,r)f_{t,j}(p,r) be the predicted gain for candidate (t,j)(t,j) after setting its process and interference scores to (p,r)(p,r) and leaving its remaining inputs unchanged. Comparing mean predictions with the zero-score baseline gives

ΔP\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{P}} =maxp∈{1,2,3}⁡1ν​∑(t,j)∈ℐIft,j​(p,0)−1ν​∑(t,j)∈ℐIft,j​(0,0),\displaystyle=\max_{p\in\{1,2,3\}}\frac{1}{\nu}\sum_{(t,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}}f_{t,j}(p,0)-\frac{1}{\nu}\sum_{(t,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}}f_{t,j}(0,0), (6)
ΔR\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{R}} =1ν​∑(t,j)∈ℐIft,j​(0,0)−minr∈{1,2,3}⁡1ν​∑(t,j)∈ℐIft,j​(0,r).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\nu}\sum_{(t,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}}f_{t,j}(0,0)-\min_{r\in\{1,2,3\}}\frac{1}{\nu}\sum_{(t,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{I}}}f_{t,j}(0,r).

ΔP\Delta_{\mathrm{P}} compares the best nonzero process level with the baseline, while ΔR\Delta_{\mathrm{R}} measures the largest predicted loss across nonzero interference levels.

We construct NN round-bootstrap datasets by sampling complete optimization rounds with replacement. PSS and RSS are the fractions with ΔP>0\Delta_{\mathrm{P}}>0 and ΔR>0\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}>0, respectively:

ψ=1N∑n=1N𝟏{ΔP(n)>0},ρ=1N∑n=1N𝟏{ΔR(n)>0}.\psi=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{\Delta_{\mathrm{P}}^{(n)}>0\},\qquad\rho=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}^{(n)}>0\}. (7)

PSS (ψ\psi) therefore measures evidence that explicit process structure improves candidate outcomes, while RSS (ρ\rho) measures evidence that suppressing interference improves them.

Adaptive representation selection.

Phase II selects among three structural representations: (a) flat forms a skill bank of independently retrievable units without an imposed execution order; (b) graph connects guidance nodes through explicit dependencies to encode the required execution order; and (c) hybrid combines an ordered core with independently retrievable auxiliary modules. Figure 2 illustrates these three structures.

The selector first uses PSS (ψ\psi) to determine whether explicit ordering is warranted. For high-PSS profiles, RSS (ρ\rho) then distinguishes graph from hybrid. RSS measures outcome evidence for harm from interference, not the prevalence of redundant guidance itself. Low PSS therefore selects flat to avoid imposing unsupported order. High PSS selects an ordered representation: low RSS selects graph to encode dependencies directly, whereas high RSS selects hybrid to preserve an ordered core while modularizing redundancy-sensitive guidance. Because PSS and RSS are bootstrap proportions, we set ζψ=ζρ=0.50\zeta_{\psi}=\zeta_{\rho}=0.50, treating a sensitivity as present when a majority of bootstrap datasets support its positive contrast. Table 1 summarizes the resulting decision rule and the permissible specialization updates for each representation.

Specialization procedure.

Phase II specializes the selected representation through iterative, validation-gated updates. At each epoch, the fixed policy model πθ\pi_{\theta} executes the current artifact on a training batch and uses the resulting trajectories and evaluator feedback to propose one revision, subject to the representation-specific update rules in Table 1. The revision may modify guidance, topology, retrieval metadata, or auxiliary modules. The candidate is evaluated against the current artifact on the same held-out examples and adopted only if it passes the Phase II validation gate detailed in Appendix A.1; otherwise, the current artifact is carried forward to the next epoch.

Experiments

Setup.

Following the evaluation strategy of SkillOpt [6], we evaluate SkillSpec on GPT–4.1, GPT–5.4 Nano, and GPT–5.4 across six benchmarks: SearchQA [7], SpreadsheetBench [11], OfficeQA [12], DocVQA [8], LiveMath [9], and ALFWorld [10]. We use each benchmark’s training split for optimization, its validation split to accept or reject candidate updates, and its complete test split only for final evaluation. We report success rate per benchmark and the macro average across all six benchmarks. Complete hyperparameters and optimization budgets are reported in Table 4.

Method comparison.

We compare against six baselines. (a) Baseline executes the evaluated model without an external skill. (b) GEPA [5] reflects on execution trajectories and retains Pareto-efficient prompt candidates. (c) Trace2Skill [27] distills trajectory-local lessons into reusable skills. (d) SkillAdam [15] uses optimization memory and adaptive update magnitudes. (e) SkillOpt  [6] iteratively optimizes a persistent skill. (f) SkillOpt-lite [13] performs file-based skill optimization with Claude Sonnet 5. We additionally report the consensus-gated Phase I output, denoted SkillSpec-I, as the paired reference for the complete Phase II stage.

Main Results

Performance across models.

SkillSpec achieves the highest average success rate for all three evaluated models: 60.41% on GPT–4.1, 48.05% on GPT–5.4 Nano, and 78.27% on GPT–5.4. These scores improve over the corresponding no-skill baselines by absolute margins of 19.93%, 19.10%, and 24.59%, respectively. They also exceed the strongest external baseline for each model by 9.57% on GPT–4.1 (SkillAdam), 3.27% on GPT–5.4 Nano (SkillOpt-lite), and 1.76% on GPT–5.4 (SkillOpt-lite). At the benchmark level, SkillSpec leads on SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, OfficeQA, and LiveMath with GPT–4.1; is best or tied-best on OfficeQA, DocVQA, LiveMath, and ALFWorld with GPT–5.4 Nano; and leads on SearchQA, OfficeQA, LiveMath, and ALFWorld with GPT–5.4, where it also ranks second on SpreadsheetBench. Even before specialization, SkillSpec-I achieves a higher overall average than any external method when averaged across all three models. This result indicates that multi-intent optimization in Phase I already provides a strong foundation, while Phase II yields additional gains on average through representation-specific continued optimization.

Paired specialization gain.

Across the 18 paired model–benchmark settings, SkillSpec outperforms its exact SkillSpec-I backbone in 13, ties in one, and underperforms in four. Averaged within each model, Phase II yields absolute gains of +3.52%+3.52\%, +0.74%+0.74\%, and +2.67%+2.67\% for GPT–4.1, GPT–5.4 Nano, and GPT–5.4, respectively; the average gain across all settings is +2.31%+2.31\%. Since each pair shares the same starting checkpoint and provenance, these results capture the overall effect of Phase II, including both representation selection and continued optimization.

Phase I Dynamics

Figure 3 suggests that accepted edits shift from behavioral contract formation to local constraint refinement as the incumbent matures. Early trajectories are shaped primarily by rewrite, which accounts for 15 of 32 accepted updates across all three models; these accepted updates occur in five of the six benchmarks. The less frequent simplify has four accepted updates, all in rounds 1–2. Later gains increasingly come from targeted changes: four of seven accepted repair updates occur after round 4, while preserve appears mainly on LiveMath and the already strong GPT–4.1 DocVQA trajectory. Appendix B.1–B.4 illustrates the same shift: the early cases restructure workflows or output contracts, whereas the later cases narrow or clarify specific exceptions.

Representation Ablation

For GPT–5.4 Nano, Table 3 reveals distinct Phase I sensitivity profiles across benchmarks. SearchQA and DocVQA share a low-PSS, high-RSS profile, indicating limited support for beneficial explicit ordering but evidence that reducing redundant or conflicting guidance is beneficial. OfficeQA, in contrast, involves retrieving relevant documents, extracting evidence, and performing calculations that depend on the extracted values. Unlike answering from supplied snippets in SearchQA or a document image in DocVQA, this workflow introduces dependencies between intermediate steps, consistent with its higher PSS and the use of Graph to encode their order. SpreadsheetBench, LiveMath, and ALFWorld share a high-PSS, high-RSS profile in the Phase I estimates reported in Table 3, motivating both process structure and interference control. Dependencies between spreadsheet operations, mathematical reasoning steps, or state-dependent actions in ALFWorld motivate an ordered core, while redundancy sensitivity motivates keeping auxiliary guidance modular.

The Phase I, equal compute control continues textual skill optimization without representation conversion, using the same number of optimization epochs and training examples as each Phase II variant.

Using only Phase I telemetry, SkillSpec selects the best-performing representation on five of the six benchmarks. On the remaining benchmark, DocVQA, it selects Flat, which trails Graph by just 0.53% (66.58% versus 67.11%). Across all six benchmarks, SkillSpec’s six-benchmark macro-average is 50.27%, above fixed Flat, Graph, and Hybrid by absolute margins of 3.36%, 2.36%, and 1.17%, respectively. All aggregates are computed from unrounded per-benchmark scores. The six-benchmark comparison supports adapting the representation to Phase I sensitivity rather than imposing a fixed structure, without consulting test outcomes during routing.

Conclusion

We introduced SkillSpec, a two-phase framework for improving LLM agents through skill optimization without updating model weights. Phase I uses consensus-gated evolution to refine reusable knowledge, while Phase II uses trajectory-derived sensitivity signals to select and optimize a flat, graph, or hybrid organization. Across six benchmarks, SkillSpec improves the average success rate over SkillOpt by absolute margins of 11.63%, 5.92%, and 3.12% on GPT–4.1, GPT–5.4 Nano, and GPT–5.4, respectively. These findings suggest that effective skill optimization requires attention not only to what knowledge an agent retains, but also to how that knowledge is structured for execution.

Appendix A Hyperparameters and Configuration

Representation decisions use only sanitized Phase I telemetry and the accepted backbone. The telemetry optimizer extracts structured observations; fixed code computes PSS, RSS, and support from them. Benchmark and task identifiers are prohibited as explicit decision features, and no test-set labels or outcomes are provided. This restriction removes direct identifiers but does not imply that semantic task characteristics are absent from the skill or trajectory.

Phase II Validation Gate

Each Phase II candidate is evaluated once on a fixed held-out selection set using the same task IDs and execution seed across epochs. The gate metric is hard accuracy. Let aea_{e} denote the candidate accuracy at epoch ee and ainca_{\mathrm{inc}} the cached incumbent accuracy, initialized by evaluating the initial Phase II artifact on the same selection set. The candidate is adopted if and only if ae>ainca_{e}>a_{\mathrm{inc}}, in which case the cached score is updated to aea_{e}. Ties and regressions retain the incumbent. This gate is distinct from the repeated paired consensus gate used in Phase I.

Appendix B Phase I Intent Examples

Below, we present representative diffs for one accepted update from each intent. Added and removed lines are highlighted in green and red, respectively, while unchanged content is omitted. Because rewrite can reorganize most of a skill, we show its principal edits rather than the full diff. To make the before–after contrast explicit, we render the append-only preserve clarification as a normalized replacement: the original rule is shown in red and the accepted rule, including the added clarification, in green. For display, Unicode punctuation is normalized to ASCII and percentage-unit wording in the simplify diff is rendered as %. No other wording is changed. Reported validation scores are mean hard accuracies over three repeats.

Rewrite

GPT–5.4 SpreadsheetBench, round 1.

Before: The skill only required checking that target cells contained the expected values.
After: The rewrite introduced an explicit reopen-and-verify procedure, distinguished formulas from computed values, and required literal, nonblank outputs in every requested cell.

Validation: 33.3%→75.0%33.3\%\rightarrow 75.0\%.

Simplify

GPT–5.4 OfficeQA, round 2.

Before: A single rule combined the bare-value requirement with an underspecified exception for units or words.
After: The update separated the two concerns and clarified that narrative scale cues are not output tokens unless the requested format explicitly includes them.

Validation: 65.3%→72.2%65.3\%\rightarrow 72.2\%.

Repair

GPT–5.4 SpreadsheetBench, round 4.

Before: The skill broadly allowed literal formula strings for formula-authoring or repair requests.
After: The repair narrowed that exception to tasks that inspect formula text and otherwise required the literal computed value.

Validation: 75.0%→77.5%75.0\%\rightarrow 77.5\%.

Preserve

GPT–5.4 SpreadsheetBench, round 5.

Before: The formula-text exception did not explicitly cover diagnostic requests that also named a destination cell.
After: The preserved rule was augmented to treat any named destination as requiring its computed value and to forbid a blank fallback.

Validation: 77.5%→80.8%77.5\%\rightarrow 80.8\%.

Appendix D PSS/RSS Estimation

This section specifies the candidate-level annotation and fixed ridge-estimation procedure used for the sensitivity scores in Table 3. It complements Equations 6 and 7: the language model supplies evidence-grounded labels, while numerical code fits the outcome model and computes the scores.

Annotation evidence and rubric

The unit of annotation is a candidate’s edit relative to its round’s incumbent skill, not the benchmark as a whole. Each record is identified by an observation_id and linked to a unified skill diff. The diff-only annotation workspace exposes observation_id, candidate_diff, and diff_file; numerical screening gains and candidate metadata are joined separately by the scorer. The annotator is instructed not to use or infer benchmark, dataset, environment, or sample identity, and to ignore intent names, acceptance decisions, optimizer summaries, tool counts, and the outer interaction format.

A process annotation requires an added or strengthened ordered prerequisite, state handoff, or conditional dependency in the solution procedure. Generic advice to “reason step by step” is insufficient. An interference annotation requires added guidance that is visibly duplicated, conflicting, irrelevant to the surrounding skill, or disproportionately overlong. A negative screening gain is not itself evidence of interference. The same four-level strength scale is applied independently to both labels, as detailed in Table 6.

The permitted interference modes are duplicated, conflicting, irrelevant, and overlong; more than one may apply. Removing redundant text does not automatically receive a positive interference label: the instruction concerns what the candidate adds. If the diff is missing or supplies no grounded evidence, the prompt requests zero strengths and an empty mode list.

The following illustrates the output schema, not a scored experimental observation:

{
  "trajectory_observations": [
    {
      "evidence_id": "<observation_id copied verbatim>",
      "evidence": "<specific evidence from the skill diff>",
      "process_structure_strength": 0,
      "interference_strength": 0,
      "interference_modes": []
    }
  ]
}

There must be exactly one observation per source candidate, with a unique matching identifier and a nonempty evidence string. Both strengths must be integers from 0 to 3; nonempty interference modes require a positive interference strength. The annotator does not output PSS, RSS, confidence, or a representation choice. The validated annotation runner allows up to three generation attempts when output fails JSON or schema validation, rather than accepting malformed output or heuristically repairing it.

Eligibility, regression, and round bootstrap

Annotations are joined to recorded candidate outcomes by identifier. A candidate enters the regression if and only if it changes the incumbent, passes patch validation, and has a recorded screen_net_gain. Zero-gain and negative-gain candidates remain eligible, including candidates rejected by the update gate. Unchanged or invalid candidates and candidates without a screening outcome are excluded. The estimator uses screening outcomes, not pooled confirmation gains or final test scores.

For Equation 5, the implementation compares the two texts after splitlines() using difflib.SequenceMatcher with autojunk=False. Each non-equal block contributes the larger of its before and after line counts. The denominator is the larger total line count, with a minimum of one for the empty-text case.

For each eligible candidate, the numerical features are

(ct,j,pt,j,pt,j2,rt,j,rt,j2).(c_{t,j},\,p_{t,j},\,p_{t,j}^{2},\,r_{t,j},\,r_{t,j}^{2}).

Each column is centered and divided by its population standard deviation; a zero standard deviation is replaced by one. The design matrix also includes an intercept and one-hot indicators for round and candidate profile, omitting one reference level for each categorical variable. There is no process–interference interaction term. With XX denoting this design and yy the recorded screening gains, the fitted coefficients are

β^=(X⊤​X+Λ)−1​X⊤​y,Λ=diag⁡(0,1,…,1).\widehat{\beta}=(X^{\top}X+\Lambda)^{-1}X^{\top}y,\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,1).

Thus the ridge penalty is one for every non-intercept coefficient, including categorical controls. The implementation solves the linear system directly rather than forming the inverse.

To evaluate a contrast, the scorer sets all rows’ process and interference strengths to the probe values, recomputes their squares, and retains each row’s edit size and categorical controls. It applies the fitted standardization, averages the predictions, and computes the extrema in Equation 6. The full-sample fit yields ΔP\Delta_{\mathrm{P}} and ΔR\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}; the bootstrap yields the positive-contrast proportions.

Sampling uses NumPy’s default_rng(42) over sorted round labels. All eligible candidates from a drawn round stay together; candidates are not independently resampled. The validated scoring runner checks that the full-sample fit and all 2,000 bootstrap fits succeed, rather than silently reporting a proportion over fewer fits. These resamples reuse existing round blocks and are not 2,000 independent experiments. PSS/RSS summarize fitted effect-sign stability, not the probability that one representation outperforms another.

Appendix E Shared-Backbone Example

To isolate organization from content, we use the same ALFWorld backbone for all three illustrations below. The source is the frozen seed-42 Phase I artifact shared by the ALFWorld ablation branches. Its Heat & Place procedure reads:

Find X →\rightarrow take X →\rightarrow go to microwave →\rightarrow heat X →\rightarrow go to Y →\rightarrow put X.

The same artifact instructs the agent to open closed containers before judging them empty, transform an object before placing it, track progress, avoid repeated-action loops, and choose only admissible actions.

Table 7 re-expresses this source content schematically. Unit names and dependency edges are introduced for exposition; these are not verbatim exports of three learned checkpoints. They illustrate representation semantics, not additional evaluation runs. All three retain the same action-format and admissibility constraints.

Observed execution evidence.

Table 8 shows one actual training episode from the archived round_00_train batch, with source identifier train:0028. Its goal is “heat some egg and put it in countertop.” Actions and zero-based step indices are retained verbatim; observations are condensed for readability. The episode contains 12 actions and ends with the environment marking the task complete. It was collected with the textual Phase I skill, not by executing each of the three schematic representations.

Reading the trace through the three representations.

The handoff from acquisition at step 6 to heating at step 8, and then delivery at step 11, makes the relevant state dependency concrete. In the Flat illustration, the transformation unit supplies guidance after acquisition without a graph-defined retrieval order. In Graph, explicit edges connect those stages. In Hybrid, the same chain belongs to the core, while container exploration or loop-recovery guidance can be supplied separately. These describe how the evidence can be organized, not measured retrieval choices for this episode. The return to the already inspected fridge at step 4 is preserved in the trace: successful completion does not imply perfect adherence to every instruction or optimal action efficiency.
